claim: IL-2/JES6-1 mAb complexes dramatically increase sensitivity to LPS through IFN-γ production by CD25+Foxp3- T cells.
source: IL-2/JES6-1 mAb complexes dramatically increase sensitivity to LPS through IFN-γ production by CD25+Foxp3- T cells

claim: Complexes of IL-2 and JES6-1 mAb (IL-2/JES6) provide strong sustained IL-2 signal selective for CD25+ cells.

claim: IL-2/JES6 potently expand Treg cells.

evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: IL-2/JES6 are effective in the treatment of autoimmune diseases.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Izquierdo et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2011; Webster et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2008).

claim: IL-2/JES6 protect against rejection of pancreatic islet allografts.

claim: IL-2/JES6 dramatically increase sensitivity to LPS-mediated shock in C57BL/6 mice.

claim: The phenomenon of increased LPS sensitivity by IL-2/JES6 is dependent on endogenous IFN-γ.

claim: The phenomenon of increased LPS sensitivity by IL-2/JES6 is dependent on T cells.

claim: The phenomenon of increased LPS sensitivity by IL-2/JES6 is not manifested in nude mice.

claim: IL-2 exerts its biological activities through binding to either a dimeric receptor composed of IL-2Rβ (CD122) and common cytokine receptor gamma chain (γc, CD132) or to a trimeric receptor composed of a dimeric one with the addition of IL-2Rα (CD25).

evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: CD25 is not involved in signal transduction.
source: CD25 is not involved in signal transduction, but increases the affinity of the trimeric receptor for IL-2 by about 100-fold (Minami et al., 1993; Waldmann, 1989).

claim: CD25 increases the affinity of the trimeric receptor for IL-2 by about 100-fold.

claim: The dimeric IL-2 receptor has a Kd of ~1 nM.
source: The dimeric receptor (Kd ~1 nM) is mostly found on memory CD8+ T and NK cells, whilst the trimeric receptor (Kd ~10 pM) is typically expressed at high levels by Treg cells, recently activated T cells and ILC2s (Boyman and Sprent, 2012; Roediger et al., 2013; Sakaguchi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

evidence: This is a logical requirement for the proposed hypothesis.

claim: IL-2/JES6 feeds back onto CD25 expression.
source: Even low expression levels should be sufficient since it has been previously shown that IL-2/JES6 feeds back onto CD25 expression (Spangler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spangler et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment with IL-2/JES6 increases the counts of CD45+ cells in the liver.
source: An interesting feature of IL-2/JES6 treatment is the increased counts of CD45+ cells (i.e. any haematopoietic cells, except erythrocytes) in the liver (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: A decent increase in counts of CD11b+CD14+ cells was found in the lungs after IL-2/JES6 treatment.
source: A decent increase in counts of CD11b+CD14+ cells was also found in the lungs (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Accumulation of CD11b+CD14+ cells in liver and lungs might significantly contribute to the pathological effects seen after LPS challenge in IL-2/JES6 pretreated mice.
source: We believe that accumulation of these cells in liver and lungs might significantly contribute to the pathological effects seen after LPS challenge in IL-2/JES6 pretreated mice, since these cells are likely to be sensitized to LPS via IFN-γ produced by CD25+ T cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Treatment with IL-2/JES6 per se induces more severe lung oedema in comparison to treatment with IL-2/S4B6.
source: Further, treatment with IL-2/JES6 per se induces more severe lung oedema in comparison to treatment with IL-2/S4B6, which could contribute to the morbidity and mortality after LPS challenge to some extent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by lung wet weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adoptive transfer of peritoneal exudate cells from mice i.p. injected with IL-2/JES6 did not increase sensitivity to LPS in adoptively transferred mice.
source: However, adoptive transfer of peritoneal exudate cells from mice i.p. injected with IL-2/JES6 did not increase sensitivity to LPS in adoptively transferred mice.
evidence: This is an experimental observation ruling out the role of peritoneal macrophages.

claim: I.v. administration of IL-2/JES6 leads to the same level of LPS sensitivity in comparison to i.p. administration.
source: Moreover, i.v. administration of IL-2/JES6 leads to the same level of LPS sensitivity in comparison to i.p. administration.
evidence: This is an experimental observation ruling out the role of peritoneal macrophages.

claim: Peritoneal macrophages do not play an important role in LPS sensitivity induced by IL-2/JES6.
source: Therefore, we can rule out the idea that peritoneal macrophages play an important role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the adoptive transfer and route of administration experiments.

claim: Treatment with either IL-2/JES6 or IL-2/S4B6 significantly increased counts of T cells in the liver.
source: We found significantly increased counts of T cells in the liver of mice treated with IL-2/JES6 or IL-2/S4B6 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: IL-2 complexes (Mw ~190 kDa) are easily accessible in the liver interstitium due to the massive fenestration of capillaries in this organ.
source: We do not know the mechanism of T cell accumulation in the liver upon treatment with either IL-2 complexes, however, we can speculate that IL-2 complexes (Mw ~190 kDa) are easily accessible in the liver interstitium due to the massive fenestration of capillaries in this organ (DeLeve, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to DeLeve, 2015.

claim: The liver and secondary lymphoid organs are the sites where increased numbers of CD11b+CD14+ and IFN-γ-producing T cells colocalize upon IL-2/JES6 treatment.
source: It seems that the liver and secondary lymphoid organs are the sites where increased numbers of CD11b+CD14+ and IFN-γ-producing T cells colocalize upon IL-2/JES6 treatment, and this feature governs LPS hyperresponsiveness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Colocalization of CD11b+CD14+ and IFN-γ-producing T cells in the liver and secondary lymphoid organs governs LPS hyperresponsiveness.
source: It seems that the liver and secondary lymphoid organs are the sites where increased numbers of CD11b+CD14+ and IFN-γ-producing T cells colocalize upon IL-2/JES6 treatment, and this feature governs LPS hyperresponsiveness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.
